scopeNotes: New text needs independent review; earlier hashes do not certify it.
Map endpoints are not historical founding or extinction dates.

The imported Apiaka polygon spans 1492 to 1500 around the upper Tapajós headwaters, consistent with the identity discussed here. It is not a verified 1492 boundary or evidence for a single kingdom. The Card does not concern similarly named peoples in other basins.

The long twentieth-century phase is explicitly approximate and groups documented disruption and rebuilding. No precise date is invented for a remembered flight, settlement foundation or every massacre.

The 1828 image and the 2009 schoolbook reproduction were visually inspected in the IHF PDF. Observation of depicted architecture is distinguished from ethnographic generalization. Manuscript copies from 1837 to 1859 are not mislabeled as all painted in 1828.

The museum booklet’s assertion that the final speaker died in 2011 is not adopted. Sousa documents subsequent work with named speakers; differences in proficiency categories, scope and dates make a timeless extinct-language label inappropriate.

Older museum project pages refer to three speakers, population estimates and pending legal processes. These are not represented as present-day counts or legal status. Recordings and videos themselves were not played.

The community account is explicitly attributed testimony. It is not a census of every Apiaká community or a basis to expose locations of isolated groups. Speculation about contact with isolated relatives is omitted.

The 2024 declaration is documented as a dated milestone, not a claim that homologation was complete. Nearby villages, peoples and territory names remain distinct. Proposed legislation is not treated as enacted repeal.

No evidence identifies a single successor polity or conquest date that can be linked to verified map geometry. Independent historical review, geometry assessment and depth certification remain pending.
